bio.en: Brandon Chu is a former VP of Product and GM of Platform at Shopify, where he helped define and scale the company's product organization, and the creator of influential writing on product management (The Black Box of Product Management / The Linear Method).
bio.zh: Brandon Chu 曾任 Shopify 产品副总裁兼平台总经理，帮助定义并扩展了公司的产品组织，也是极具影响力的产品管理著作（The Black Box of Product Management / The Linear Method）的作者。

summary.en: Brandon shares mental models for product and platform strategy, including “shipping is a feature” and the discipline of making high-leverage decisions with limited information. He discusses scaling product and engineering at Shopify, aligning teams around crisp context, and why small teams that start small avoid wasted engineering resources. The conversation is a masterclass in product judgment, platform thinking, and developing product managers.
summary.zh: Brandon 分享了产品与平台策略的思维模型，包括“交付即功能”（shipping is a feature），以及用有限信息做出高杠杆决策的纪律。他讨论了在 Shopify 扩展产品与工程、围绕清晰上下文对齐团队，以及为何小团队从小起步能避免工程资源浪费。对话堪称产品判断力、平台思维和培养产品经理的大师课。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: So way back in university, I kind of grew up actually in the era where people really wanted to work on Wall Street still. So I actually came up through the finance ranks and stuff like that. And I worked in industry at Kraft Foods of all places for about four years, but how I kind of broke into product management is I got really bored that really quickly. And I started moonlighting and bootstrapping a startup on the side and it was called Tunezy and it helped YouTube musicians at the time, which were blowing up. This is kind of when Justin Bieber was becoming famous by doing webcam cover music and stuff like that. And we helped YouTube musicians monetize their fan bases by offering fan experiences at their tour stops. And so this was really early. This is before YouTube even had a music category. And so my co-founder and I, neither of us were technical, but we were pretty good at pitching. (05:08): And so we kind of entered a lot of startup competitions and we got some funding and some office space and we quit our jobs literally the weekend after we won that. And then fast forward three and a half, four years, we never really made a really big company out of it, but we kind of soft landed sold the company. And I'd say that's my first foray because my job as a co-founder there was really to work with engineering and design. And it was through that experience that I learned everything about product and I got a lot more technical too. I was able to do a little bit on the front end. And so from that, after the acquisition and the integration that parlayed that into product management career basically. So I joined a growth stage startup in Canada, in Toronto called FreshBooks, which is still around today. (05:50): They're a Series D company now. And I kind of learned the chops of product management there because the folks there were X Microsoft 15 years, really technical, process-oriented and framework heavy product management. And I had my just scrappy entrepreneurial experience. So I kind of hardened my PM skills through that over about four years. And then I joined Shopify the week of the IPO actually. So that's almost seven years ago and it was one of the largest companies I ever worked at. I had 500 people even then at least because I'd been in startups prior. So I thought maybe the story's over.- But as I met Tobi through my interview process, I realized that that was definitely not true. And it obviously is not true now. (06:30): So yeah. I've been seven years there, various PM roles, areas of the product and then eventually really started to build some domain expertise around platform management and developer ecosystems and kind of grew my career there. And through that domain, became product director and then a VP of product. And then in classic Shopify form, I completely threw it all away and started something a little different inside the company 18 months ago. So now I lead what we call product acceleration, which is the team that does all of Shopify's investments and then [inaudible 00:07:02].
turns.zh: 早在大学时代，我成长于一个人们仍热衷于在华尔街工作的时代。因此，我在金融领域一路打拼，还曾在卡夫食品等公司工作了四年左右。但我真正进入产品管理领域的原因是，我很快就感到厌倦了。于是我开始兼职创业，创办了一家名为Tunezy的初创公司，专注于帮助当时风靡的YouTube音乐人。当时贾斯汀·比伯正凭借网络摄像头翻唱音乐走红，我们通过在巡演站点提供粉丝体验，帮助YouTube音乐人变现。这还是YouTube尚未推出音乐类别的时候。我和联合创始人虽然没有技术背景，但很擅长推销项目。我们参加了许多创业比赛，获得了资金和办公空间，获奖后的周末就辞掉了原工作。三年半到四年后，虽然我们没能打造出大型公司，但成功退出并出售了公司。我认为这是我的首次尝试，因为我在那里的职责主要是与工程和设计团队合作。通过这段经历，我掌握了产品管理的所有要领，技术能力也得到了提升，甚至能处理一些前端工作。收购整合后，产品管理生涯就此开启。我加入了加拿大多伦多的初创公司FreshBooks（至今仍在运营），现已完成D轮融资。在那里，我学习了专业的产品管理方法——团队成员都是微软15年资深人士，注重流程和框架。他们丰富的经验让我迅速成长，历经四年磨练，最终在Shopify IPO前夕加入。如今已过去近七年，这是我服务过的最大型公司。当时我手下就有500名员工，毕竟我此前在初创公司待过。原本以为故事就此结束，但在面试Tobi时，我意识到这远非终点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. So I was looking at your LinkedIn and just hearing this story, especially the Shopify piece, it's a pretty incredible trajectory. And imagine a lot of people listening to this may be like, "Shit. How do I follow a similar path? How do I do it Brandon did." Do you have any advice about what it was that helped you, either habits, skills, behaviors that helped you get to where you're today that maybe newer PMs could learn from?
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。我看了你的领英主页，听你讲述这些经历，尤其是Shopify的部分，简直令人惊叹。想必很多听众会想：“天啊，我该如何走出类似的职业路径？如何效仿布兰登的成功之路？”你能否分享一些帮助你走到今天的习惯、技能或行为方式，或许能给新晋产品经理带来启发？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: I think what I learned over the arc of my career is that especially when it comes to product management specifically, it's a lot of the hard skills that PMs are known for, so organizational, analytical, good communication, even technical skills. There's sort of table stakes and commodities to be an entry level PM. And to be clear, it's not easy to be a PM. It's not an entry level job. And so that is no knock on that. I'm saying to grow beyond that though, I think domain expertise can take you a little bit further like if you're an amazing payments PM or you have some really nuanced knowledge and whatever, 3D modeling or something like that. (08:05): But I think ultimately to have the highest trajectory and what certainly was a tailwind for my career was you guys have to lean into those founder skills. And so things like being a great storyteller, how to get the most out of people around you, foster creative and motivated teams and know how to make really, really hard high conviction decisions that actually can't be solved. You got to take a leap of faith and how to do that and bring teams through that type of ambiguity and then how to lead by example and have accountability when you make those choices. So I found that ultimately, those really became the things that were limiters for some careers I observed and then were definitely propelling for a lot of the people that made it to high level of leadership.
turns.zh: 我认为，在我的职业生涯中，我领悟到的一点是，特别是就产品管理而言，人们通常关注的是产品经理所需的硬技能，比如组织能力、分析能力、沟通能力，甚至是技术技能。这些都是入门级产品经理必须具备的基础技能。说实话，做好产品经理并不容易，这绝不是一份入门级的工作。但我要说的是，若想突破现有框架，深厚的领域专业知识能助你走得更远。比如，你若是出色的支付产品经理，或者在3D建模等领域拥有深厚的专业知识，都会为你加分不少。（08:05）但我认为，最终能实现职业飞跃的关键在于，必须培养创始人般的领导才能。比如，如何成为优秀的讲故事者、如何充分激发团队创造力与积极性，以及如何在面对无法解决的难题时做出高信念度的艰难决策。这些能力需要你具备跳出固有思维的勇气，在团队陷入迷茫时能带领大家渡过难关，并在决策后勇于承担责任。我发现，这些能力正是许多职业生涯停滞不前的瓶颈所在，而对那些能晋升至高层领导职位的人来说，它们却成了推动职业发展的引擎。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And I know you wrote a lot about a lot of these things, which we'll talk about your writing, which I'm a huge fan of and I have been a fan for a long time. But before we get into those, I want to chat a little bit about Shopify and your experience at Shopify and just understanding the product culture at Shopify. As an outsider, Shopify feels like an incredibly strong product culture. And I know a lot of amazing PMs that work there and even outside PMs, just generally amazing people. What would you say are some of the defining characteristics of how teams build product at Shopify maybe that are different from how other companies approach product?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我知道你写过很多关于这些内容的文章，我们稍后会聊聊你的写作风格——我一直是你的忠实粉丝，而且追随已久。但在深入探讨这些话题之前，我想先聊聊Shopify、你在Shopify的经历，以及对Shopify产品文化的理解。作为局外人，Shopify给人的感觉是拥有极其强大的产品文化。我认识许多在那里工作的杰出产品经理，甚至是非产品经理的优秀人才。你认为Shopify团队在产品开发方面的哪些特质与其他公司有所不同？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: Shopify has an incredibly strong product culture. Whether it's uniquely different, I can't know for sure, but I would say I'd start with, it's a highly technical company. That's not unique, but it's just something that should be known about Shopify. When I joined, all project management was just in GitHub, just commenting on poll requests and even marketers in order to augment or upload a blog post, you'd have to commit and deploy it. So there was no breaks given for folks that didn't want to touch code and stuff like that. I think it was very much and this all stems from Tobi, a very well renowned developer in the Rails Core community and it all kind of flowed from him. (09:59): And so because of that, I think everyone in the company had their hands really deep in the product regardless of what function you are, which brings me the second thing I think is really awesome with Shopify, when it comes to how the product org works, it's that we don't actually put the product org on a pedestal as the only people that can have an opinion about the product or should be listened to when we think about what should be built. There's sort of an understanding of Shopify that everyone at the company from engineers to support, to sales, everyone's responsible for product thinking and it's not just the area for a small group of PMs. (10:38): And so that's some of the foundations of it. And again, all stems from Tobi. I'd say the last one is that this comes from the fact that we have Canadian roots. And I say that actually in a way that's almost opposite of the stereotype when it comes to tech anyway. There has been a lot of failed tech companies in Canada and no company that's ever truly been global. And so ambition and a founder mentality has been something that we've architected the culture of the product team around. And so 30 to 40% of the PM team are ex founders either through failed startups or through acquisition. (11:15): And this is really important to us for obvious reasons about just versatility and grit and growth mindset but then also we are building a platform for other entrepreneurs, whether they're merchants on our platform or developers to build their own stuff. And so we have a lot of empathy for our customers through that. And so the way this is all kind of coalesced is the one liner job description we give to PMs as they come in is "Your job is to help teams ship the right thing at the right time in the right way." And it really comes down to two main concepts. There's help teams. So it's like servant leadership. You're not necessarily the CEO of the product. You're not dictator. Everyone's responsible for product thinking and you're there to help the team get to ultimately the right thing. And that is what you are accountable for.
turns.zh:
Shopify拥有极其强大的产品文化。是否称得上独树一帜，我不敢断言，但我可以说，这首先源于它是一家高度技术导向的公司。这并非独特之处，但确实是Shopify值得一提的特质。我加入公司时，所有项目管理工作都通过GitHub完成——无论是开发者、市场营销人员还是其他成员，若想添加或上传博客文章，都必须进行代码提交和部署。这意味着那些不愿接触代码的人根本没有喘息的机会。我认为这一切都源于Tobi，他是Rails核心社区备受尊崇的开发者，由他推动了这一切变革。

（09:59）正因如此，Shopify的每个员工，无论身处何种职位，都深度参与产品开发。这也让我想到了Shopify在产品组织运作方面最令人赞赏的第二点：我们从不将产品团队置于神坛地位，认为只有他们才有权对产品发表意见或决定开发方向。相反，公司上下从工程师到客服、销售，每个人都肩负着产品思维的责任，这并非仅限于产品经理的小圈子。

（10:38）这正是基础理念所在。这一切又都源于Tobi。我想强调的最后一点是，Shopify源自加拿大基因。说到科技行业，加拿大素来被贴上失败标签，鲜有真正全球化的科技巨头。因此，雄心壮志和创始人精神始终是我们产品团队文化的核心支柱。PM团队中30%至40%的人曾是创业者，或是失败的初创公司创始人，或被收购的公司创始人。

（11:15）出于显而易见的原因——多元化、韧性、成长型思维——这对我们至关重要。同时，我们为其他创业者搭建平台，无论是平台上的商家，还是开发者自建应用。通过这种方式，我们对客户心怀同理心。PM团队入职时得到的简明职位描述是：“你的职责是帮助团队在正确的时间、以正确的方式交付正确的产品。” 这归根结底基于两个核心理念：一是服务团队。二是以身作则。你不是产品的CEO，也不是独裁者。每个人都负有产品思维的责任，你的职责是帮助团队最终达成目标，这也是你需要为之负责的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that definition. In practice, do you give PMs a little bit more sway over decisions or do you try to keep it completely equal amongst functions?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个定义。实际操作中，你们会给PM们更大的决策权，还是努力保持各职能部门的平等？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: Actually, I think it depends on the level. So I think as you go to towards more the junior PMs and the ICs, there is a much bigger emphasis on balanced decision making between all the Kraft's user experience and engineering, of course. And then it's more when you get to director level or above, that's when there is more emphasis put on where the PM wants to lead, because ultimately, it becomes a pure strategic function at that point and that is your only job. Your only job is to say, "We need to go there and my ass is online for us going there." And so that is something I think we matured into. There was obviously lots of tension as we grew of, "Hey. We used to collaborate, but now you're saying we have to do this thing." And it's like, well, actually, the company, the context changed, my role changed and we have to do something and it has to be someone's job to make that choice. So it's a bit of both is the answer.
turns.zh: 实际上，我认为这取决于职位层级。举例来说，当你晋升为初级产品经理或初级交互设计师时，必然会更加强调在用户体验与工程开发之间做出平衡的决策。到了总监级别及以上职位时，重点则会转向产品经理的战略方向，因为此时产品管理已完全转变为纯粹的战略职能，唯一的职责就是明确方向并全力推进。这正是我们逐渐成长的历程。在发展过程中，我们曾面临诸多矛盾——“我们过去常常协作，但现在你却要求我们必须这么做。”但实际上，公司环境和职位角色都发生了变化，必须有人来做出决策。这就是两者兼顾的答案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Spending a little more time on decision making in general at Shopify. Is there kind of a framework or a specific process you guys use to make bigger decisions?
turns.zh: 太棒了。Shopify在整体决策层面投入了更多精力。你们在做重大决策时，是否有特定的框架或流程？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: What we do have is an annual planning cycle basically, we call investment plans and it's for fairly large SWOTs to the organization. I'm talking like 20% chunks of all of Shopify consolidated under a VP here and there to put forward a vision for what that team's going to accomplish that year, whether that is a directional change or even specific outcomes in some cases. And we spend time aligning with both Tobi, the rest of the C level exec team, even sometimes the board on what that is and what headcount may go with that and what not. But that's sort of the main arc of planning. What happens after that is just chaos, all the teams underneath and like I said, one fifth of Shopify may be moving towards one investment plan, that's at this scale almost 2500 people. Right? So they're all now chaotically moving towards those end goals and iterating through ideas good and bad. (14:15): And so this is actually where Shopify is a really hard place too, because we do this because we recognize a couple things. One is it's important that we set broad direction, so everyone can put their energy towards the right place. But we also want a place where we're hiring smart people so that they can figure out what to do. And we also know that in software and in tech and in this world, things change so rapidly. So don't even kid yourself that we're going to plan out everything we're going to have to do for the next year to get there. And so we set this directional kind of outcome and vision based kind of north star for where we want to go. Then product directors start to basically shoot their shot and say, "This is how my group can contribute to those things. Here's what we're going to try to commit to in the next quarter basically." (14:58): And it's through that almost back and forth, the trust battery thing that I was talking about plays in. Again, they're selling it to their peers, the engineering directors. They're selling it to the VPs. They're selling it to the broad team as well to get momentum behind it and to say, "You know what? This feels right. Let's start doing that." But what's really amazing and also difficult about Shopify though is we're pretty good at never falling into sunk-cost fallacy. So we'll throw it all away anytime if the world changes. Right? (15:29): And so that's why it's actually a really tricky place for a lot of folks because there are cases and it's happened to me many times where it's just like you're building three, six months into something and it's just not important anymore or the world changed. And so that's kind of how the sausage gets made. And it really comes down to giving teams the agency, giving product folks at certain levels the responsibility to make a bet, and then having the humility to understand that soccer's hard, the world changes and that we always have to ask ourselves this is the most important thing that we can do right now.
turns.zh:
我们的确有一个年度规划周期，我们称之为投资计划，主要针对公司层面的重大战略评估。我所说的投资计划，通常涉及Shopify内部20%的资源，由各部门副总裁牵头，为团队设定年度目标，无论是战略方向调整，还是具体成果达成。整个过程中，我们会与托比（Tobi）、其他高管团队，甚至董事会保持沟通，共同确定规划方向、人力配置等核心要素。但这只是规划阶段的主线。

接下来就是混乱的执行阶段。各部门团队会根据投资计划行动——在Shopify这样拥有近2500名员工的公司，五分之一的团队可能都在朝着同一目标前进。于是大家都朝着既定目标努力，尝试各种想法，修正错误路径。

（14:15）这也正是Shopify面临挑战的核心所在。我们之所以这样做，是基于两点考量：一是制定宏观方向至关重要，让团队聚焦核心任务；二是吸引优秀人才加入，让他们有自主发挥的空间。毕竟在软件科技领域，变化瞬息万变。我们不可能预设好未来一年的所有行动方案。因此，我们会设定一个指引性的愿景目标，然后让产品总监们各抒己见："我的团队将如何为此贡献力量？接下来一个季度我们将重点推进哪些项目？"（14:58）这整个过程中，信任机制至关重要。产品总监需要向工程总监、VP等团队成员反复阐述方案，激发团队热情，形成共识："这条路是对的，让我们行动起来。"但Shopify的独特之处在于，我们善于规避沉没成本陷阱。一旦环境变化，我们随时会调整策略。（15:29）这也正是许多人对Shopify心生敬畏的原因。曾有过多次经历：团队投入三六个月精力，成果却因市场变化而失去意义。这就是Shopify的运作逻辑。关键在于赋予团队自主权，让产品负责人承担决策风险，同时保持谦逊，承认世界变化无常，时刻反思当下最重要的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so important. A lot of companies just want to avoid upsetting people, want to avoid creating chaos. And it's so important to always be rethinking even if it's like we just put a plan together, maybe we should change it because things have changed. And so I'm not surprised Shopify is really good at this.
turns.zh: 这太重要了。许多公司只想避免动荡，避免混乱。但真正重要的是持续反思。即便刚制定完计划，也要根据新形势调整策略。我对Shopify在这方面的卓越表现毫不惊讶。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: To give an example, during COVID, this cultural resilience we had to change was so vital because all of a sudden, these grandiose ideas and visions we had for 2020 didn't matter and what mattered was like, "Oh, shit. Retail businesses are going from a hundred percent to zero." It's like 0% revenue overnight. And how do we help a brick and mortar store across the street now do order online and pick up it in store? How do we do that? How do we throw away everything? This is what matters now. Let's try to ship three things in the next month that matter." And that's very jarring, I think, unless you have a culture that just understands that can happen any day and it kind of gets excited by those.
turns.zh: 举个例子，在新冠疫情期间，我们不得不改变的这种文化韧性至关重要，因为突然间，我们对2020年的宏伟构想和愿景都变得无关紧要，真正重要的是：“天啊，这些零售企业从百分之百的营业额一下子跌到零。”一夜之间收入归零。我们要如何帮助街对面的实体店铺开展线上订单并到店自提业务？该如何从头开始？这才是当下最重要的。我们要在接下来的一个月里推出三项对业务至关重要的功能。”我认为，这真的很令人震惊，除非你的企业文化能理解这种随时可能发生的变局，并从中激发活力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd love to actually hear whatever you could share on the COVID period of Shopify and just what folks did to work through that.
turns.zh: 我很想听听您对Shopify在新冠疫情期间的应对措施，以及团队是如何应对挑战的。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: Yeah. Through all the roadmaps, we asked ourselves, "Hey. Our customers, their livelihoods are at risk right now." And this is when no one knew it would actually be a tailwind for e-commerce. Right? We didn't know the severity of COVID. It could have been a really, really bad pandemic from a death rate perspective. So no one's betting like, "Oh, everyone's going to stay home for two years and everyone's going to buy stuff online." Everyone's like, "Okay. All our customers are going to go to zero, unless we help them figure out how to actually survive through this." (17:40): And so of course, online only merchants or merchants who were well established online have that infrastructure. There wasn't supply chain issues yet. So they're good. The focus then turned, of course, to all these both hybrid brick and mortar online customers and customers that are only brick and mortar. And so we did all those things. Some restaurants and grocery stores on the platform, how do we help them do exactly that buy online, pick up at the curb? How do we help them launch buy gift cards now at a discount so that basically you can, as a consumer, help these companies stay afloat. If you recall back in 2020, that was a huge thing. Buy gift cards at the restaurant you like, because if you don't, it might not exist.
turns.zh: 是的。在整个路线图规划过程中，我们不断自问：“嘿，我们的客户现在生计面临威胁。”当时没人预料到这场疫情会成为电商行业的机遇，对吧？我们当时根本不了解新冠疫情的严重性。它本可能是一场死亡率极高的灾难。所以没人会天真地认为“所有人都会在家隔离两年，然后全都转向线上购物”。大家都清醒地意识到，除非我们帮助客户渡过难关，否则所有客户都将面临倒闭风险。（17:40）当然，纯线上商家或早已建立线上业务的商家具备相关基础设施，当时供应链问题尚未显现，所以他们情况尚可。随后，我们的重点转向了线上线下混合模式的客户，以及纯实体店铺客户。我们为此采取了多项措施。比如，如何帮助平台上的餐厅和杂货店实现线上下单、路边自提？如何让他们推出折扣礼品卡促销活动，让消费者能以优惠价格支持这些企业生存。（2020年的经历令人难忘）买喜欢的餐厅礼品卡吧，因为如果不买，可能这家店就消失了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I did that a bunch. I remember. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我当时经常这么做。记得很清楚。是的。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: So these things exist on Shopify in apps because they were never really mission critical, but now it became really mission critical. So all of a sudden we're trying to gear 500 people towards ship gift cards, which sounds like a really small feature, but it's pretty hard when you have millions of merchants and hundreds of millions of consumers using your platform every day, ship it in two weeks. And so it became war time truly. And yes, Tobi got way more involved, as did Craig Miller, our CPO at the time. And we went down from trying to ship maybe the 40 things that quarter to three and nothing else mattered. And that became the rhythm of the company for almost that entire year.
turns.zh: 这些功能最初在Shopify平台上只是可有可无的附加项，但疫情期间却变得至关重要。比如，动员500名员工在两周内上线礼品卡功能，看似是个小功能，但当你面对数百万商家和数亿日活用户时，要完成这项任务实属不易。整个公司瞬间进入战时状态。托比（Tobi）和当时的首席产品官克雷格·米勒（Craig Miller）投入了大量精力。从每季度40项任务缩减至三项，其他所有事务都让位于当务之急。这种节奏几乎贯穿了整个2020年的运营。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. How long did that kind of war time period last internally?
turns.zh: 哇。这种战时状态在公司内部持续了多久？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: I'd say the edge came off a little bit I think mid 2021. It wasn't that long ago actually, maybe about a year ago that it started. I would say it never really left war time per se, but everyone sort of adjusted to it. And so many other things were happening because we had offices before and we made the decision very early in the pandemic to say, "We're never going to have offices again. We're a digital by default company. Hire anywhere in the world, but let's make sure we have really great infrastructure." And so there was so many things happening inside the company that just changed. It really changed overnight. Shopify, the experience, the culture of the company changed overnight. And so it's hard to say when it stopped, it just evolved.
turns.zh: 我觉得2021年中左右，情况开始有点变化了。其实这事儿没过去多久，大概一年前就开始了。我觉得我们从未真正脱离战时状态，但大家都逐渐适应了这种状态。公司内部也发生了很多变化，因为我们之前有实体办公室，但在疫情初期就决定："我们再也不需要实体办公室了。我们要成为一个默认远程办公的公司。可以在全球任何地方招聘，但要确保基础设施完善。"所以公司内部发生了太多变化，一切几乎一夜之间就变了。Shopify的体验和公司文化也一夜之间发生了转变。所以很难说这种变化何时结束，它只是在不断演变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wanted to actually ask about that and so I'm glad you brought that up. The fact that Shopify's been very remote friendly for a long time, I imagine it's rooted in the fact that it was founded in Ottawa and it's probably hard to hire the scale of people that you're all hiring out of Ottawa. And I imagine there was an advantage to having a lot of that experience working remotely in this new modern world. And I also imagine wasn't easy still, but what I'm curious about is what sorts of things have you learned about working remotely that you can share that other companies can maybe learn from Shopify's experience?
turns.zh: 我正想问问这个问题，很高兴你提到了这一点。Shopify长期以来一直支持远程办公，我想这源于它在渥太华创立的事实。在渥太华很难招聘到大规模的员工队伍。因此，在这个新兴的现代世界中，积累远程工作经验无疑是一种优势。我也知道这并不容易，但我想知道的是，你们在远程工作方面学到了哪些经验，可以分享给其他公司借鉴？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: Finding enough that in-person still matters. It does. And that doesn't mean we're rolling back at all the fact that we're remote only, but what we've done is we've actually instituted with something we call bursts. So bursts at Shopify are the ability for your team generally maybe once a quarter or whatnot, to just come together to do really high velocity creative work together, to hang out together. And so we've gone pretty far on this where we actually have in-house built web and mobile apps that allow teams to one click, say I have 20 people. We want to do a burst in Laguna Beach and then click the button and then flights get booked, hotels get booked, food is taken care of. No one has to pay any. There's no expenses that go back and forth. The app itself helps you check into those places. (21:24): And we have really cool experiences. And in France and Ireland, I'll leave a little bit to the imagination, but it's really cool. So we started allowing kind of that as the world opened up for travel and now teams are doing it all the time. I'm going next week actually to one with our team.
turns.zh: 我们发现面对面交流仍然很重要。确实如此。这并不意味着我们要回归全远程办公的模式，但我们引入了一个叫做“Burst”的机制。在Shopify，Burst让团队成员每季度或更频繁地聚在一起，开展高强度创意工作，增进团队凝聚力。我们为此开发了内部网页和移动应用，一键操作即可。比如我想在拉古纳海滩举办Burst活动，只需点击按钮，航班、酒店、餐饮等所有安排都由系统完成，无需任何费用报销。应用还能自动签到。（21:24）在法国和爱尔兰的Burst活动就不方便透露太多细节了，但确实很棒。随着旅行限制放宽，我们开始推广这种模式，现在团队经常举办Burst活动。我下周就要和团队去参加一个活动了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You just do a personal burst. I just want to go to The Bahamas first.
turns.zh: 你可以直接组织个人Burst活动。我想先去巴哈马。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: You can try. We've done other things too, because you spoke in Bahamas. I actually worked out of the Caribbean for five weeks in March. And because we also had a policy that we instituted that said for 90 days out of the year, you can work in any country you want. And so what we tried to do with a remote only world is we tried to turn all the weaknesses on its head and to say, "Okay. Well, we can't see each other every day, but let's remember all the ways that sucked from a commute perspective and even when you were together, if you were just working in your desk and never even talking to each other, that wasn't great. So why don't we just optimize for the stuff that was amazing about it and make it super easy and fun?" (22:23): And that's what bursts became. And then, hey, we have amazing infrastructure now. We can work with global teams 24/7/365. Why are we forcing people to stay in a location? The reality is the 98 thing is mostly because of a tax thing, but ultimately, we have the infrastructure that people can just log in from wherever. And so why not lean into.
turns.zh: 你们可以试试。我们也做过其他尝试，因为你提到了巴哈马之行。我在三月份曾在加勒比地区工作了五周。当时我们制定了一项政策，规定一年中有90天，你可以在任何你想去的国家工作。对于远程办公模式，我们试图彻底扭转其弱点，并思考："好吧，我们无法每天见面，但回想一下，通勤带来的种种烦恼，即便大家同处一室时，如果只是各自埋头工作而从不交流，那也不算理想。何不充分利用其优势，让远程办公变得轻松有趣呢？"（22:23）于是"Burst"项目应运而生。如今我们拥有出色的基础设施，可以全天候与全球团队协作。为何还要强制员工固定办公地点？实际上98天规则主要源于税务考虑，但归根结底，我们已具备让员工随时远程办公的技术支持。既然如此，为何不顺势而为呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. This is really interesting. I love that your answer to how to work remotely better is get together more often, which I hear a lot from companies, but I love that you've built this infrastructure to enable it. I'd love to hear a bit more of how this product works. Is it all in-house? Any advice I guess, for anyone trying to build something like this?
turns.zh: 是啊，这真的很有趣。我喜欢你提到的通过增加面对面交流来优化远程办公体验的做法。虽然很多公司都这么说，但你们实际构建了支持这种模式的基础设施，这点很棒。我很想了解这个产品是如何运作的。它完全由内部团队开发吗？对于那些想开发类似产品的公司，有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: I hate saying that it is all in-house because that is not easy, really accessible for midsize or below companies, but basically, you initiate an event called the burst. You can choose what type of thing you're trying to do, whether it's a pure work thing or you want to have a little bit of activity and social aspects of it. There's different locations, depending on how many people are going that are available to you. There's a booking system. If you choose to do something a little more low key and just meet in, let's say a major city, then we actually allow you to access our old offices. So the leases didn't go away. So we had to use these offices for something and these offices have now completely been retrofitted. They're beautiful. And they are amazing. I wouldn't even say co-working spaces. They're just community spaces now that you go in and you can use them and you have everything. There's food there. There used to be there's board rooms and whatever you want to have your little offsite or whatever it may be. (24:01): And then there's a rating system after. How is the burst there? There's a whole team that manages the logistics of all these things. So that it's very just like we don't have managers all over the company trying to figure out flight plans and stuff like that. And yeah. It's great. And we also get the data to be able to see, hey, what teams haven't been together in a very long time? And ask the lead, "Hey. Why is that? Is it because everything's good and people are busy? Maybe something about a baby or something like that and they can't get around." Or is it a prompt that, "Hey, maybe your energy is low as a team, it's time to get together." So that's the benefit I think of having built that app and that infrastructure is that we get to really understand how it's actually helping.
turns.zh: 我不太想说它完全是内部开发的，因为这对中小型企业来说确实不太容易实现。但基本上，用户可以发起名为"Burst"的活动。你可以选择纯粹的工作模式，或者加入一些社交元素。根据参与人数，会有不同类型的场地可供选择。预订系统会自动匹配最合适的场地。如果你选择更低调的活动，比如在某个大城市见面，我们甚至允许使用原有的办公室。租约并未终止，所以这些办公室被重新改造，变得美观且实用。我甚至不愿称之为共享办公空间——现在它们更像是社区空间，提供全套设施。里面有餐饮区，过去还有董事会会议室等设施，方便举办小型离线会议或其他活动（24:01）。活动结束后会进行评估。有一整个团队负责所有后勤事务，这样公司就不必安排专人协调航班安排等事务了。确实很棒。我们还能获取数据，查看哪些团队已经很久没有聚在一起了。然后询问负责人原因：是因为一切顺利大家都很忙？还是因为有孩子出生等私事无法出席？又或者是团队士气低落，需要组织聚会了？我认为开发这个应用和基础设施的好处在于，我们能真正了解它带来的实际价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by PostHog. PostHog offers a suite of product analysis tools, including funnels, heat maps, session recording and experimentation all in one easy to use platform. PostHog is open sourced so you can host it on your own infrastructure, which means that you have control over who has access to your data and makes regulatory compliance a breeze because you don't need to send user info to third parties. PostHog's app system works seamlessly with your data warehouse, both for importing and exporting data, which enables you to bring your data into one place and easily understand user behavior across a range of touchpoints. If you'd like to learn more, check them out at posthog.com/lenny. Just one last technical question about this product because it's so cool. Is there an API that just books flights or does it just send you to kayak and you book these flights?
turns.zh: 本期节目由PostHog赞助。PostHog提供一套产品分析工具，包括漏斗分析、热力图、会话录制和实验测试等功能，所有这些都集成在一个易于使用的平台上。PostHog是开源的，因此您可以将其部署在自己的基础设施上。这意味着您可以控制谁能访问您的数据，并轻松满足监管合规要求，因为无需将用户信息发送给第三方。PostHog的应用系统与您的数据仓库无缝协作，支持数据导入和导出，让您能够将数据集中管理，并轻松理解用户在各个接触点上的行为。如果您想了解更多信息，请访问posthog.com/lenny。最后再问一个关于这款产品的技术问题，因为它太酷了。它有直接预订航班的API吗？还是说它只是把用户导向Kayak然后由Kayak来完成预订？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: I don't know the exact answer, but I would imagine. So we also use trip actions inside of Shopify and I'm pretty sure they have an API, so probably we've done something directly with them. So they've handled all the really complex stuff, but we probably use them for the booking action itself.
turns.zh: 我不确定具体答案，但我猜应该有。我们在Shopify中也使用旅行动作功能，我很确定他们有API，所以我们可能直接与他们合作了。所以他们处理了所有复杂的部分，但预订动作本身可能还是由我们来完成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Sweet. This is super interesting. I've never heard of this. I want to transition to talk a little bit about your writing. So your writing is how I originally discovered you. It's on the top, I don't know, 1% of most useful, actionable, interesting writing on the Kraft Food product management. I still refer to it often and share it with people all the time and it says a lot, because it's a little older at this point and you've kind of slowed down the writing. I'm curious when you were in that writing phase, a lot of people want to write, a lot of people know that it's good for many reasons, but a lot of people don't do it. What would you say worked well for you when you were in that period to get you to actually get stuff written and also just create time for writing?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。这真是太有趣了。我从未听说过这个。我想转到您写作的部分来谈谈。您的写作是我最初发现您的地方。它在Kraft Food产品管理领域的实用、可操作和有趣的文章中排名前1%。我仍然经常参考它，并经常与他人分享。这很能说明问题，因为它已经有点过时了，而您写作的频率也降低了。我很好奇，当您处于那个写作阶段时，很多人想写作，很多人知道写作对很多方面都有好处，但很多人却不去做。当您处于那个写作阶段时，您做了什么有效的事情来促使您真正写出东西，并且为写作腾出时间？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: Yeah. Well, first of all, thank you. That's super generous. I think if you say I'm in the top 1%, then Lenny, you're definitely in the top 0.1 or 0.01% and so kudos to you.
turns.zh: 是的。首先，非常感谢您这么说。如果您说我在前1%，那么Lenny，您肯定在前0.1%或0.01%，这太值得称赞了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I aspire to be you.
turns.zh: 我渴望能像您一样。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: And also thank you for being generous saying I've slowed down a bit. The reality is I haven't written anything since 2018. So when I reflect on it, I think I wrote those in a time where I was figuring out a lot of stuff while I was executing. And I wanted to crystallize in my mind some mental models and frameworks that had been forming somewhat intuitively. The funny thing about those posts when I reflect on them and I've rarely reread them, but every once in a while, someone shares an excerpt and I end up kind of rereading and be like, "Do I even believe this still?" But when people read them, they think like, "Oh, they're learning from someone who's figured it out for a while and now they're sharing it later in their career or something." (27:21): But the reality is, and maybe this resonates with you. It's like I figured out everything in those posts at the exact moment I wrote them. It was the writing process itself that actually allowed me to solidify those mental models and those frameworks in my mind. And so I wasn't ahead of the game in any way. It was just I think I really wanted to disambiguate the chaos in my mind about what my job was. And it took me to really interesting places. And I think it was also coupled with two things, which was I had a really good career trajectory at the same time so I could actually observe. I wasn't too mired in being a PM one for five years and then moving. I was moving through things really quickly so I was able to contrast things because it was literally like, "Oh wait, three months ago, it was that. Now, how do I change?" (28:03): And that, of course, is not just me, but it's also at Shopify I grew so much during that time. Right? We grew seven years ago. I came at just under 500 people. Were over 12,000 people today. And so it was a really formative time for the whole company and definitely myself. And in terms of just writing well and shipping quality posts and stuff like that, I'm sure this resonates with you. You just got to put in the work. You got to put in a lot of hours. I put 40 hours into a post, do it on the weekends or I brain dumped a first draft of it in two hours and drew 38 hours of editing or getting feedback from people or drawing some diagrams that I put in there. But it was that process. (28:44): And I think it was such an amazing thing to learn how to do is to just sit and write for five hours and reread the thing and actually also get feedback from people. Don't be so afraid to share raw, early thoughts and for it to not make sense but then when you give to someone objective and they read it, they'll be like, you really learn things about how you put a narrative together in your mind versus how someone actually reacts to it. And so that fearlessness to get a lot of feedback, I think, was something I developed through those years.
turns.zh: 还要感谢你大方的说我最近写得少了。但事实上，我自2018年起就没写过什么东西了。回想起来，我写那些文章时，正处于摸索阶段，边实践边理清思路。我当时想把一些逐渐形成的思维模型和框架固化下来。每次回看那些帖子（我很少重读），总有人分享片段，我才重新翻看一遍，心里想：“我现在还认同这些观点吗？”但读者们却会觉得：“哇，他们是在向已经成功的人取经，现在分享经验罢了。” （27:21）但现实是，也许你能感同身受。我写那些文章时，很多观点都是在当下突然领悟的。正是写作过程本身，让这些思维模型和框架在我脑中逐渐成形。所以我并没有先人一步，只是想理清自己工作的混乱局面。这段经历也让我收获了两点：一是当时的职业发展轨迹让我能边实践边观察。我没有深陷PM角色五年后才跳槽，而是快速切换赛道，所以能对比不同阶段的差异。二是Shopify的快速发展为我提供了绝佳的成长环境。七年前我们只有500人，如今已突破12000人。这段经历对公司和个人都意义非凡。写作方面，保持高质量输出，关键在于投入时间。我曾花40小时写一篇文章，周末完成初稿后，又花38小时润色、收集反馈、绘制图表。正是这样的过程，让我学会了如何静下心来写作，重读修改，再虚心听取意见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everything you said 100% resonates with my approach. There's a quote I often think about. It might be Hemingway or might be misattributed to Hemingway that "I don't know what I think until I've written it down." And that's exactly how I feel like it's a forcing function to help you actually figure out something. And that's exactly how I started.
turns.zh: 你说的每句话都和我现在的方法不谋而合。我常想起海明威的一句话：“直到写下来，我才知道自己在想什么。” 这正是写作能帮助你理清思路的迫使功能，也是我写作之路的起点。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: And it's a release too, because when you write it down, you just kind of release it from your mind. It's not floating around there because I'm scared to lose it or something like that. And you kind of just now you cleared your mind and you can actually think. You build on top of that knowledge into something else.
turns.zh: 这也是一种释放压力的方式，因为当你把想法写下来时，它们就从你的脑海中被释放出来了。它们不再在那里漂浮不定，因为你害怕会遗忘之类的。而现在你清理了思绪，就能真正思考了。你可以基于这些知识进一步拓展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly how I felt when I first started writing. I just want to get these things out of my head before I forget them partly to help crystallize something that I can actually hold onto that won't fade away.
turns.zh: 这正是我刚开始写作时的感受。我只想把这些想法从脑海中清除出来，免得忘掉，这样就能把一些东西具象化，让它们不至于逐渐消逝。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: Okay. How many posts have you written now?
turns.zh: 好的。你现在写了多少篇帖子了？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think probably 300.
turns.zh: 我觉得大概有300篇。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: 300. How are you still motivated to, or where do you even find things to write about now?
turns.zh: 300篇。那么你现在怎么还能保持动力，或者说你从哪里能找到新的写作素材呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I have a endless list of things I want to write about. And partly, these ideas come from founders and PMs that are constantly sending me questions that they have. And the way I see it is until nobody has any more questions to ask about starting a company, building a product, driving growth, I'm going to have things to write about.
turns.zh: 所以我有一长串想写的内容。部分灵感来自于创始人和产品经理，他们不断向我提问。就我看来，只要没人再对创办公司、产品开发、增长策略等问题感兴趣，我就总有可写的内容。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: That's amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it feels like that's an endless supply. The bigger challenges, it gets harder and harder because the easier stuff is getting knocked out. And so that's the bigger challenges. Things remaining are things that take more time, more research, more digging, things like that. But at this point, yeah, I've been doing it for over three years and still got plenty of ideas.
turns.zh: 而且感觉这是一个无穷无尽的素材库。越难的挑战越难攻克，因为越容易的部分已经被解决了。所以这些才是更大的挑战。剩下的都是需要更多时间、更多研究、更多探索的事情。但到目前为止，是的，我已经做了三年多，还是有很多想法。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: [inaudible 00:30:48].

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's no better motivator than somebody paying you for your content and [inaudible 00:30:51].
turns.zh: 而且没有比有人为你的内容付费更棒的动力了[00:30:51的不可听部分]。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: Well, it's a symbiotic relationship.Right? All those questions and feedback from your subscribers and whatnot is fodder for the next thing that you're going to give. And I think that's an amazing relationship.
turns.zh: 嗯，这是一种共生关系，对吧？所有订阅者和其他人的问题和反馈都是你下一次创作的素材。我觉得这是一种很棒的关系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly right. I wanted to ask you, do you think every PM/leader should spend time writing? Who should? Who shouldn't? What are you feeling on that?
turns.zh: 确实如此。我想问你，你认为每个产品经理/领导者都应该花时间写作吗？谁应该写？谁不应该写？你对此有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: I think yes. Even if it's not to be publicly shared or whatnot, I think ultimately, especially in a increasingly digital world and increasingly remote world, you've got to be able to articulate yourself. Again, even going back to that process of writing and what it does for how you understand what you're saying, you owe your team, your peers, your stakeholders that level of clarity. So even if you write it and throw away, you've created a clarity in your mind and you can articulate it as such and people deserve that. And I think that if you're going to be a really good PM, you have to have that skill.
turns.zh: 我认为应该。即使不打算公开分享，我也觉得在一个日益数字化、日益远程化的世界里，你必须能够清晰地表达自己。再说回写作的过程，以及它对理解自己所说内容的帮助，你对团队、同行、利益相关者都有责任做到清晰明了。所以即使你写了又扔掉，你也在脑海中建立了清晰的思路，可以清晰地表达出来，人们理应得到这样的清晰度。我认为如果你想成为一个优秀的产品经理，就必须具备这种能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What impact have you seen as a result of your writing that you've done?
turns.zh: 你写作带来的影响有哪些？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: Oh, it's honestly been the most important thing I've ever done in my career unbelievably. And it's had probably two really interesting effects. One is that as Shopify grew and when we were going through hyperscale, you probably recognize this from your Airbnb days as well but people are falling from the sky. Every day there's 20 new people showing up and you having been there already, now you got to figure out what all these people are doing and give them all the context and all these types of things. And how do you even teach them the culture and the ways that you work and stuff like this. And so one amazing, and just the context, I'm really old at Shopify now. I'm like 99.1% tenure. So I'm ancient at the company.
turns.zh: 哦，说实话，这确实是我职业生涯中做过的最重要的事情，简直难以置信。它产生了两个非常有趣的影响。首先，随着Shopify的快速发展，当我们经历超大规模扩张时——你们可能从Airbnb的经历中也熟悉这种情况——每天都有20个新员工加入。当时你已经在公司待了一段时间，现在你得去了解所有新人的工作内容，为他们讲解公司背景和各种事务。更重要的是，你要如何向他们传授公司的文化、工作方式以及其他相关内容？说起来，我在Shopify已经待了很久了，资历堪比“元老级”——我的在职时间占比达99.1%，在公司里算是“活化石”了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a stat that shows up? Is there a little dashboard?
turns.zh: 有没有相关数据可以展示？有没有小型仪表盘之类的？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: There is in our little internal wiki thing.
turns.zh: 在我们的内部维基系统里有相关数据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:32:35].

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: So I'm literally ancient in the company. And so one of the amazing effects that the writing had was that people that would join my team already knew how I thought. It was pretty onboarded a lot of the PMs that would join my team because obviously, they're going to look for who their leads is and Google that a bit and they see a posting and be like, "Is this person legit or not or whatever?" And so I didn't really even have to onboard many people in so many ways. They kind of knew how I thought about the world. And also, even when I was in Shopify and writing those posts, there's so much noise in Shopify. It's a very chaotic place. There's so many exciting things happening that it is very hard to tell a 200 person PM org, "Stop. Pay attention to this idea." (33:20): So I actually found that writing externally and getting momentum externally was a better way to influence internally what was happening, to the effect that Tobi would read my post here and there and he'd be like, "Great post." And I'd be like, "Hey, daddy loves me." But no, but seriously, it would help build my trust battery with Tobi because of the way that those posts gain traction and whatnot. So it has had an incredible, incredible impact on my personal career. And also I think it has brought a lot of really great people to Shopify. Literally every week a new PM messages me and says like, "Hey. I just joined. Your post had a lot of influence on me or whatever. And I'd love to meet up and blah, blah, blah." But that has been amazing and it's so rewarding. Another small example, this wasn't in the black box, product management like general cannon or whatever per se, but I was working on the integration product with Facebook Messenger via Shopify. (34:16): And as part of our launch, I wrote just to get more, because we're a very small company than them. So we're using any angle we can. So I'm writing on my personal blog about this thing that we launched and David Marcus, who's now leading their blockchain crypto stuff, but he was CEO of PayPal for a while. And then he came in to lead all the Facebook's payment stuff and Messenger. Oh, sorry. Kind of lead Messenger. Anyway, he shared it on his Facebook and on Twitter. And then that blew up and all of a sudden, the CPO of Shopify, Craig or whatever, now starts thinking I'm legit even though... Because someone of his caliber was also sharing these things, about a product that we built and whatnot. So it was just really interesting how these little things had an impact on how people perceive you and thus how much impact and momentum you can create inside a company.
turns.zh: 这么说吧，我在公司里可真是老资格了。写作带来的一个惊人效果是，加入我团队的人往往已经了解我的思维方式。由于他们肯定会去搜索我的头衔、浏览相关帖子，然后发现我写的东西，自然会想：“这人靠谱不靠谱？”所以很多时候我根本无需特别培训新人——他们本就对我的世界观心知肚明。即便我在Shopify写那些帖子时，那里的信息量太大，环境混乱，各种激动人心的事件层出不穷，要想让200人的产品管理团队停下脚步关注某个想法实在太难了。（33:20）所以我发现，通过对外写作并积累影响力，是影响公司内部动态的绝佳方式。比如托比偶尔会读到我的帖子，然后说：“很棒。”我会开玩笑说：“老爸爱我。”但说真的，这确实能提升我和托比的信任度，因为这些帖子能获得关注等等反馈。这对我的职业生涯影响巨大，而且还吸引了许多优秀人才加入Shopify。几乎每周都有新加入的产品经理主动联系我，说：“嘿，我刚加入。你的帖子对我影响很大。”这种反馈真是太棒了。再举个小例子，这不算产品管理领域的经典案例，但确实很有趣。我当时负责Shopify与Facebook Messenger的整合产品。（34:16）作为产品发布的一部分，我写了篇博文宣传这个新产品。大卫·马库斯（David Marcus）现在负责Facebook的区块链加密业务，但他曾担任PayPal首席执行官，后来接手Facebook的支付和Messenger业务。哦，对不起，应该是负责Messenger的工作。不管怎样，他在Facebook和Twitter上分享了这篇文章，结果引发了轰动。突然间，Shopify的首席产品官克雷格（Craig）之类的就开始认可我了，尽管……因为他这种级别的人物也分享了我们产品的信息。这真是太有趣了，这些小举动能影响人们对你的看法，从而在公司内部创造巨大的影响力和势头。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you think about it, say you spend 40 hours on that post, what are or why that is spending a week or two writing something and the impact that could have on your perception within the company on your future career opportunities and even just people joining the company and that are going to work for you. They're like, "Oh my God, I'm going to work for Brandon Chu. I'm so excited."
turns.zh: 仔细想想，你花40小时写那篇帖子，能产生什么效果？花一两周时间写东西，最终对你的职业生涯、加入公司的员工以及他们对你的看法产生巨大影响。人们会说：“天哪，我要为布兰登·朱工作了。太兴奋了。”

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: I'd say even if it never got picked up, the ROI is already huge because it just again helps you refine how you talk about the work and the decisions, but that aside, it accelerated my career probably a decade.
turns.zh: 即便帖子从未被广泛传播，投资回报率也已经很高了。因为这能帮助你优化对工作的阐述和决策过程。更不用说，它还加速了我的职业发展进程，大概缩短了十年时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really good point. You should not be focused on this needs to go viral for this to be worth the time because I find that the more you think about that, the less well it does because that becomes the wrong intent.
turns.zh: 嗯，你说得太对了。你不应该把重点放在内容必须走红才值得花时间创作上，因为我发现你越是纠结于这个问题，效果往往越差，因为这会偏离正确的创作初衷。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: Yeah. Well, to be perfectly transparent about it, it is a factor in why I stopped writing. It had gained so much traction and I had become an exec now at Shopify and I was so busy at them. I was like, "I don't have the time to make this thing as good as it was. And I'm not even going to put another post out because I don't want to disappoint people." That's a real thing. I think you're probably better conditioned with this having written 300 posts now. I think you're a machine, but for me, it was like, I would put one every couple months maximum or something like that. And so when I lost the time, I had kids and all these types of things, it seemed insurmountable to prioritize.
turns.zh: 是啊，说实话，这也是我停止写作的原因之一。那篇文章获得了极高的关注度，而我现在已经是Shopify的高管了，工作非常忙碌。我当时想：“我没时间把这件事做得和以前一样好了。而且我甚至不打算再发布新文章了，因为不想让大家失望。”这就是现实情况。我觉得你现在写了300篇文章，应该对此更有经验了。我觉得你简直是个写作机器，但对我来说，最多每隔几个月写一篇文章就已经很费劲了。所以当我没时间写作，又有了孩子等等各种事情要处理时，要把写作列为优先事项简直难上加难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wanted to ask, what's your favorite thing that you've written? Which piece is your favorite?
turns.zh: 我想问一下，你写过的最喜欢的文章是什么？哪一篇最让你自豪？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: I don't know if I have a favorite, but the one that always I'd say has overall had the most traction or just constantly, even to today, people still tweet about or message me, whatever, was the one about making good decisions as a PM. Basically, the short of it is, the first thing it argues is that the most important thing to figure out when you're dealing with any decision is actually figuring out how important that decision is. Since we're faced with hundreds of decisions in any given moment around the product or whatever, and that we're only human and we can only prioritize a few, you got to figure out the importance of them so you can prioritize. And so it talks about things like either decision reversible or not. Does it affect a lot of users in a material way or not, stuff like that, ways to prioritize them basically. (37:22): And then it kind of argues that okay, given the fact that we only have limited time and that the most important decisions are so much more important than the other 98, 99 of them, you should basically spend all your time on those very few important decisions. And for all other decisions, you should just literally just go with whatever your gut is or delegate it because you're only human and your gut is going to be right a decent amount of time too. And so just make those fast so that you can keep the team velocity high. You don't ever want to be a blocker, that's the other tension and then spend all your time on these few critical decisions.
turns.zh: 我不知道有没有最喜欢的，但有一篇一直以来反响最好的，甚至到现在还有人会在推特上@我或者给我发消息的，那就是关于产品经理如何做出正确决策的。简单来说，核心观点是，当你面对任何决策时，最重要的是先弄清楚这个决策的优先级。毕竟我们每天都要处理数百个产品相关的决策，而人力有限只能处理少数几个，所以必须分清主次。例如，某个决策是否可逆？是否会对大量用户产生实质性影响？等等，通过这些标准来确定优先级。（37:22）然后文章强调，鉴于时间有限，而最重要的决策比其他99个重要得多，你应该把所有精力投入到这几个关键决策上。其他决策就随心而动或者授权他人处理，毕竟人无完人，你的直觉往往能帮你做出正确选择。这样就能保持团队的高效运转，避免成为阻碍进展的因素，最终把精力专注于少数关键决策。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Would you say that's still generally the way you work looking back at that post?
turns.zh: 回头看那篇文章，你觉得现在你的工作方式还是基本沿用了这些思路吗？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: Yeah. Definitely is still the way I work. I probably do it too much in terms of me doing my job here and there.
turns.zh: 是的。这仍然是我现在的工作方式。尤其是在我日常工作中，也会严格遵循这些原则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: It's like, "Oh, that isn't important." If you take overtime too, you get weathered down about what's actually super dire versus not. And once you've had a few battle scars of things that you thought were going to ruin everything, your career, your reputation, blah, blah, blah, and then actually nothing happened, you just start to raise the bar about what's actually important.
turns.zh: 就像“哦，这个不重要”。如果你加班太多，久而久之就会对什么是真正紧急的事情失去判断力。当你经历过几次以为会毁掉一切、毁掉事业、毁掉声誉的危机，结果却无事发生后，你就会重新设定对重要事情的标准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. We're definitely going to link to that in the description for this episode. Is there a post that you wish you had written or want to write if you have the time?
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。我们肯定会把它链接到本期节目的描述里。你有没有希望自己写过但没写出来的文章？或者如果有时间的话想写的？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: I've been wanting to write literally for three years. It'll probably be really long, but just a huge post about being a platform PM as opposed to product PM. And there's so many interesting differences in the ways that you have to think about prioritization. And I even told a story about it's a big cultural change too, that you have to affect people way beyond your team. Now you have to also work and you have to tell us to work multiparties. So you're building a, let's say a developer platform that they're building apps. Okay. Now there's multiple stakeholders. So the developers building these apps that are going to be consumed by these businesses, these merchants, and these apps also may be presented to end buyers. There's now three constituents and there's all these crazy things around policy, data sharing, just tension between which side gets economically rewarded for doing what. There's a lot of really interesting things. (39:33): And so one day I hope to write something about that and that's even on just the pure strategy and kind of economic view of it. But then there's also a super fascinating product design and engineering problems of just like, okay, you have this web app or whatever, and you want apps to exist in it. Well, how are they going to exist in it? Right? Okay. Are you just going to let them put their link in there and then it opens up a new tab into that other product that's kind of lame? That's basically a Facebook comment of a link, or are you going to allow the actual third party product to exist inside of your product and how are you going to do that? Is it going to be an eye frame? Well, that's kind of janky. (40:11): If it's going to be deeper, then now we're talking about direct data integration. We're talking about maybe your app serving UI on behalf of that app, but then some of the data comes from the third party server and it gets really, really interesting in terms of user experience and whatnot and it's actually quite common in our life that we don't think about it. (40:29): So when you long press on an app on your iPhone and it has a shortcut list of things you could do quicker. Right? Okay. Say if you long press your email app, it'll probably say create new email as one of them. That's an extension. That's iOS saying, "Hey, Gmail app. I'm going to give you the ability to actually deep link this experience into your app through our operating system." Right? Someone actually had to design that idea, that user experience and we just take it for granted because that's how it works. Right? But there's so many crazy decisions there about, well, if you go too far, you give Google too much control there and they could do some really messed up stuff. Or if you don't go far enough, then it's really just lame. It's not actually powerful. And so it's a really interesting domain.
turns.zh: 我有三年时间一直想写一篇文章了。可能会写得非常长，但这会是一篇关于平台产品经理与产品产品经理差异的巨作。优先级排序的方式有诸多不同之处，这需要深思熟虑。我甚至还讲过一个故事，说明这是一个巨大的文化转变——你必须影响到团队以外的人群。现在你不仅要管理开发团队，还要督促他们与多方合作。比如说，你在搭建一个供开发者构建应用的平台。好的，现在有多个利益相关方。开发者们构建的应用最终会被企业、商家使用，这些应用可能还会面向终端用户开放。现在有三个主体参与其中，还有各种关于政策、数据共享的复杂问题，以及各方在经济回报分配上的博弈。这些都非常有趣。（39:33）：所以我希望有一天能写一篇关于这些内容的文章，纯粹从战略和经济视角出发。但还有一些超级吸引人的产品设计和工程难题。比如，你有一个网页应用，想要让其他应用在其中运行。那么这些应用该如何存在于你的平台中呢？直接在应用内放置链接，用户点击后跳转到其他产品页面？这太简陋了，就像Facebook评论中的链接提示。或者让第三方产品直接嵌入你的平台？这又会引发诸多技术挑战，比如如何处理UI交互、数据整合等问题。（40:11）：如果要做得更深入，就涉及到数据直连。比如你的应用通过iOS系统提供UI界面，但数据却来自第三方服务器。这在用户体验方面会带来很多挑战，而我们往往习以为常，认为这很自然。（40:29）：比如在iPhone上长按某个应用，系统会弹出快捷菜单。好的，比如长按邮箱应用，可能会出现“新建邮件”选项。这就是扩展功能，iOS系统允许邮箱应用通过系统深层链接到你的应用。有人专门设计了这样的用户体验，而我们却视为理所当然，因为这就是默认操作。可其中却有诸多决策陷阱。比如，如果做得太深入，可能会让谷歌获得过多控制权，引发隐私问题。做得不够深入，又会显得功能不足。这真是个复杂的领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm glad you touched on this because this is exactly where I wanted to go next.
turns.zh: 很高兴你提到了这个话题，因为这正是我接下来想探讨的方向。

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to chat about the PM career track, but maybe before we get into that, I know you haven't written this post, but for someone that's designing a platform or an ecosystem, is there any kind of just guiding frameworks or rules of thumb that you've come to to help you make some of these decisions that you talked about?
turns.zh: 我想聊聊产品经理的职业发展路径，但在深入探讨之前，我知道这篇文章不是你写的，但对于那些正在设计平台或生态系统的人来说，是否有一些指导性的框架或经验法则，可以帮助他们做出你提到的那些决策？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: I actually say the first thing is as a PM, your psychology has to really change around your own validation. So usually, you can build a product, ship it, customers tell you if it's good or not. The cycles for platform work are five to 10 odd times longer. You're maybe changing something on the infrastructure level, then opening up an API and then doing an alpha period for the API where developers now build on that and test things. And then you move into a beta. And then finally, two years later, some end customer actually uses that app, right, for this. And you're not designing actually the end user's experience. You're designing a canvas for developers to build their own creative ideas on. And it's just a very different type of work. And so I would say that's the first thing psychologically is be prepared for those much longer cycles. (42:29): Surround yourself with people on your teams that find ways to enjoy that process and also find ways to celebrate rewards along the way like we would, not rewards, but celebrate shipping things along the way. When that API went into alpha, there's no press release, but how do you make the team feel amazing about that work? Right? You have to tell the big narrative about this is going to change how merchants actually get different apps in these areas or whatnot. And here's some of the crazy things that we're seeing in the early adoption, et cetera. So that's my main thing on psychology. I'd say in terms of preparing yourself, you really have to think about before you even get into the technical or design execution of any particular platform area, really think about the principles behind the platform that you're building. So an example, and then a contrast with Shopify's, in Amazon's platform, I'm making this up, but I assume that a pretty big important intro principle is that if there's ever a toss up between deciding between the seller and the buyer, the consumer, we're going to decide with the consumer. Right? (43:40): That's why every time you refund something on Amazon, anytime you got a complaint, send you another one. Right? They made that trade off to be a consumer focused platform and obviously, that's been amazing for them, but you also hear the contrasting stories of sellers that are really pissed off Amazon that have ruined their businesses and whatnot. So not to hate on that, but that's a second order effect of that decision. In Shopify's case, we are here to support entrepreneurs and businesses in making their dreams come true and creating independence. And that is sometimes at the cost of developers on our platform. And so sometimes we may make a data policy change saying, "Hey. It's more important that the merchant has access to this data across apps. And it's important that actually you push that data back in Shopify so that you don't hold that data back so that this other app can't use it." (44:33): And now we're sending the same end customer two marketing texts when they've already opted out of marketing texts or something like that. And so this is where you have to understand those principles and the stack rank of the constituents there to be able to make good policy and design choices. And I think it's something that if you're not conscious of early as a platform PM, you will blow up some stuff or there will be some bad instances that come up or you'll get blocked by the CEO or whatever on the day before it launches, which has happened to me.
turns.zh:
实际上，我认为首要之事是，作为产品经理，你的心态必须真正转变，适应自身产品的验证周期。通常，开发一款产品并上线后，客户会告诉你它是否优秀。但平台产品的周期要长得多得多——可能需要五到十倍的时间。首先，你可能在基础设施层面进行调整，然后开放API，接着进行API的α测试阶段，开发者基于此进行开发和测试。接下来进入β测试阶段，最终在两年后，一些终端用户才会真正使用这款应用。这时候你设计的并非最终用户的体验，而是为开发者提供一个创作平台。这完全是两种截然不同的工作模式。因此，我认为心理层面的首要准备就是要适应这些漫长的周期。

（42:29）：在团队中围绕自己，找到能享受这个过程的人，并找到途径在过程中庆祝成果。比如API进入α测试阶段时，虽然没有发布新闻稿，但如何让团队为此感到振奋呢？你必须讲述宏大的叙事——比如这将改变商家获取不同应用的方式等等——并分享早期用户的疯狂反馈。这些就是我对心理层面的主要见解。我想说，在准备阶段，你必须在深入技术或设计任何特定平台领域之前，先思考所构建平台的基本原则。以Shopify为例，与亚马逊形成鲜明对比。亚马逊的平台原则是，在卖家和消费者之间产生纠纷时，优先保护消费者。这就是为什么亚马逊每次退款、处理投诉时都会先向消费者倾斜。显然，这种以消费者为中心的决策策略对亚马逊非常成功，但你也能听到卖家被平台坑惨、生意毁掉等反面案例。这不是要贬低亚马逊，而是这种决策的二阶效应。而Shopify的使命是支持创业者和企业家实现梦想、创造独立性。有时这意味着要以开发者为代价。比如我们可能会调整数据政策，规定"商家跨应用访问数据更重要"，或者"必须将数据回传至Shopify，避免其他应用无法使用"。（44:33）：现在我们会向已经取消营销短信订阅的用户发送重复短信。这些都需要你理解这些原则，并在各利益方中进行权衡，才能做出明智的决策。如果作为平台PM早期不注意这些问题，最终可能会搞砸局面，或遭遇CEO否决等困境，我自己就经历过这样的情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, no. This sounds like a very hard place to be in an organization, building a platform, building an ecosystem like this. You went into the platform world pretty early when you got to Shopify. And I know a lot of PMs think about, "Should I go platform? Should I go user facing product?" Do you have any advice for folks that are trying to decide which path to take? And is it even a one way door? Is it easy to go to a different direction later?
turns.zh: 哦，不。这听起来在一个组织中、在构建平台、构建这样的生态系统时，处境相当艰难。当你加入Shopify时，就很早地踏入了平台领域。我知道很多产品经理都在思考：“我该选择平台路线吗？还是选择面向用户的产品？”对于那些正在决定走哪条路的人，你有什么建议吗？这是一条单行道吗？之后再转向其他方向容易吗？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: That's a really tough question. I think if you have any particular interest in the types of problems that you solve, I'd give you a little snapshot of the things you think about as a platform PM. If that stuff gets you really interested, then follow that guy. I don't think it's either, or I don't think one is better than the other. I think they're completely different types of problem domains. I don't think it's also a one way door. I'd say even if you do primarily user facing or consumer facing side of the product, you're going to be consuming things on some platform somewhere, whether it's an internal API or a third party or whatnot. So you're going to experience platforms good and bad. Right? And so you'll learn about it. And then alternatively on the platform side, you're going to be designing the canvas and you're going to see what gets built there and you're going to learn what are good and bad bounds of not a single user experience, but a universe of user experiences that are possible. (46:26): If you create a UI kit or something like that, you're going to see the good and the bad that comes out of that UI kit being given to the third party ecosystem and you'll learn about consumer. And so I also think oscillating between them is an amazing experience too, because there are really long cycles and platform work. And sometimes it's nice to ship and iterate and grow week over week and talk to your users about every single feature that you're shipping every other week. And that's so fun in different ways. And so I think having both is actually the right goal in both experiences.
turns.zh: 这真是个很难回答的问题。我认为，如果你对自己要解决的问题类型有特定兴趣，我可以简要介绍一下平台产品经理需要考虑的方面。如果这些内容能让你真正感兴趣，那就朝着那个方向发展。我不认为这是一个非此即彼的选择，也不认为其中一种方式比另一种更优。我认为它们是完全不同类型的解决问题领域。我也不认为这是一条单行道。我会说，即使你主要负责面向用户或消费者的产品，你也会在某个平台上使用其他服务，无论是内部API还是第三方服务。所以你会体验到好的和不好的平台。对吧？另一方面，在平台方面，你会设计平台框架，观察在上面构建的应用，并了解单个用户体验和可能的多元用户体验之间的优劣之处（46:26）。如果你创建了UI套件之类的东西，你会看到将该套件提供给第三方生态系统后产生的优缺点，还会了解消费者的需求。因此，我认为在两者之间切换也是一种很棒的体验，因为平台工作周期很长。有时每周都能发布和迭代，看着每两周发布的每个新功能与用户互动，这种感觉也很有趣。因此，我认为在两种体验中兼顾两者才是正确的目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To zoom out a little bit and as a final question, if you could suggest just one thing for PMs to do to help them level up in their career and just do better, what would that be?
turns.zh: 再宏观一点，作为最后一个问题，如果你能给产品经理们一个建议，帮助他们在职业生涯中提升自己、做得更好，会是什么？

turns.speaker: Brandon Chu
turns.en: Everyone has so many different backgrounds, but I'd say overall, based on most PMs that I've met, I'd say, look, it is hard to do when you are a PM somewhere, but do a legitimate side hustle, found a company on the side and learn everything else. Because I think sometimes you're in this silo of your feature, your area or whatnot. And you forget what it means to sell something to a customer, what it means to support a product, what it means to ship something and get destroyed because it doesn't even work or something like that. And so I think it humbles you a bit. It reminds you of how hard it is to build software and how many people it takes to do that well. And especially if you're not in technical, really lean into it and build something simple, learn how to build something simple for yourself, demystify the technology. (48:03): That experience will take you far. I love telling people that literally don't even know what HTML is or something like that, which I was one of those people that from right now over the weekend, you could build a clone of Twitter using a tutorial on Rails or something like that. You can do it. You may not know everything that's actually happening, right? But you could actually get that deployed and it'll work and it'll blow your mind that you did that. And I think once people break through that wall, when they're nontechnical, I think the momentum builds from there and so the side hustle and then also break technical walls or obscurity is what I would recommend.
turns.zh: 每个人背景各异，但综合我接触过的大多数产品经理来看，我想说，当你身处某个公司担任产品经理时，要想同时兼顾正职和副业，建立自己的公司并学习其他技能确实不易。因为有时你会深陷于自己负责的功能模块或领域中，忘记了向客户销售产品、支持产品运作、交付成果却遭遇失败等现实挑战。这能让你保持谦逊，深刻体会到软件开发的艰辛，以及成功背后所需的团队协作。（48:03）：这种经历将助你走得更远。我常对那些连HTML都不懂的人说——我自己过去也是这样——只要利用Rails等教程，你就能在周末快速搭建出Twitter的克隆版。你能做到的。你或许不完全理解底层逻辑，但至少能让产品上线并正常运行，这种成就感会让你惊叹不已。一旦非技术人员突破了这个壁垒，势头便会水涨船高。因此，我建议大家先从副业入手，突破技术障碍，破除行业迷雾。

turns.en: Awesome. I love that advice. It's kind of like a microcosm of create your own little business and do all the things and break out of your little box that you're in. Maybe as a PM, where can folks find you online and how can listeners be useful to you?
